# Distributed Consensus and Coordination: Technical Brief

## 1. Raft

**Leader election.** Each node is in one of three states: follower, candidate, leader. Time is divided into **terms**, monotonically increasing integers that act as a logical clock. A follower that doesn't hear from a leader within a randomized **election timeout** (randomization is the key mechanism to avoid split votes) becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and sends **RequestVote RPCs**. Each node persists `votedFor` per term so it votes at most once per term. A candidate becomes leader on receiving votes from a majority (**quorum**).

**Log replication.** The leader appends client commands to its local log and replicates them via **AppendEntries RPCs**, which double as heartbeats. Each log entry carries the term in which it was created. The **Log Matching Property** (if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, all preceding entries are identical) is maintained by having AppendEntries include `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm` consistency checks; mismatches cause the follower to truncate and the leader to retry with earlier entries. An entry is **committed** once it's replicated to a majority, at which point the leader advances its `commitIndex`.

**Safety / election restriction.** Raft's **Leader Completeness Property** guarantees committed entries appear in all future leaders' logs. This is enforced at election time: RequestVote includes the candidate's last log index/term, and voters refuse their vote if the candidate's log is less up-to-date (lower term, or same term but shorter log) than their own. Combined with quorum intersection, this ensures a candidate that wins has every committed entry from the previous leader.

**Stale leader detection.** Every RPC carries the sender's term. A leader that discovers a higher term in an incoming RPC immediately steps down to follower, preventing a partitioned-off old leader from making progress once a majority has moved on.

**Membership changes.** Raft's original paper specifies **joint consensus**: the cluster transitions through a configuration `C_old,new` in which agreement requires majorities from both the old and new configuration simultaneously, guaranteeing **quorum overlap** at every point and ruling out two disjoint majorities committing conflicting entries. In practice, most production implementations (etcd, Consul) instead use the simpler **single-server-change** restriction, adding or removing one member at a time, which is provably safe without joint consensus because old and new majorities are guaranteed to overlap when membership changes by one node at a time.

**Log compaction.** Because the log grows unboundedly, Raft uses **snapshotting**: a node serializes its full state machine state, discards log entries up to that point, and transfers snapshots (via InstallSnapshot RPC) to lagging followers instead of replaying the full log.

## 2. Paxos

**Basic Paxos.** Solves single-value consensus among proposers, acceptors, and learners. Phase 1 (**Prepare/Promise**): a proposer picks a **proposal number** (ballot number) `n` higher than any it has used, sends Prepare(n) to a quorum of acceptors; an acceptor replies Promise(n, acceptedValue) if `n` is higher than any it has seen, promising not to accept any proposal numbered less than `n`. Phase 2 (**Accept/Accepted**): if the proposer gets promises from a quorum, it sends Accept(n, v) — where `v` is either its own value or the highest-numbered already-accepted value returned in the promises (this is critical for safety) — and acceptors accept unless they've since promised a higher `n`. A value is **chosen** once accepted by a quorum. Safety follows from **quorum intersection**: any two quorums share at least one acceptor, so a higher-numbered proposal is forced to adopt any already-chosen value.

**Why Basic Paxos alone doesn't give state machine replication.** Basic Paxos decides a single value. Running independent instances per log slot, with multiple proposers competing for each slot, risks the **dueling proposers** livelock (repeated Prepare rounds with ever-higher ballot numbers preventing any Accept from completing) and does not by itself provide an efficient, ordered, durable replicated log. **Multi-Paxos** is the practical extension: elect a stable **distinguished proposer/leader** (via a leader-election sub-mechanism, often itself a lighter-weight Paxos round or a lease), and once a leader is stable it can skip Phase 1 for subsequent log slots (since its ballot number already dominates), sending only Phase 2 Accept messages — this is what production systems (Chubby, Spanner's underlying log) actually implement.

**Fast Paxos.** Reduces end-to-end message delay by letting proposers send values directly to acceptors in a **fast round**, bypassing the leader, at the cost of requiring larger **fast quorums** (more than a simple majority, sized so any two fast quorums intersect in a majority) to resolve collisions when multiple proposers race in the same round; collision recovery falls back to a classic round.

**EPaxos / Cheap Paxos contrast.** **Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos)** removes the stable-leader requirement entirely: any replica can opportunistically propose a command, and ordering between commands is determined by tracking **interference/dependencies** between commands rather than imposing a single global sequence, achieving leaderless operation with lower latency when commands don't conflict across geographically distant replicas. **Cheap Paxos** reduces the steady-state number of replicas needed to tolerate f failures (using 2f+1 acceptors but only f+1 active at a time, with standby replicas activated on failure) to lower hardware cost at the expense of a more complex reconfiguration path on failure.

## 3. Lease-Based Coordination

A **lease** is a time-bounded, exclusive grant of a right — to act as leader, to serve cached data, to hold a lock — issued by a granter to a holder, valid until an expiration time. Leases bound the blast radius of partitions and crashes: a dead or partitioned holder automatically loses authority once its lease expires, without requiring the granter to detect the failure explicitly.

**Clock assumptions.** Lease safety depends on bounded clock drift between granter and holder (or more precisely, bounded *message delay and clock skew* relative to the lease duration): the granter's notion of "expired" must be reachable only after the holder's own clock would also consider the lease expired, or inconsistent dual-ownership can occur.

**Renewal, expiration, and the zombie-leader problem.** A lease holder periodically renews before expiration. The dangerous case is a holder that **stalls** (e.g. a stop-the-world GC pause, OS scheduling delay, or network partition) past its lease expiry without noticing, and resumes believing it still holds leadership — a **zombie leader**. If it then issues writes against a downstream resource, those writes can race with a newly elected leader's writes, causing silent corruption.

**Fencing tokens.** The standard fix is a **fencing token**: a monotonically increasing number (often the lease epoch or term) issued with each lease grant. The holder must present this token on every write to the protected resource; the resource rejects any write bearing a token lower than the highest it has already seen. This converts a liveness bug (stale leader doesn't know it's stale) into a safety guarantee enforced at the resource, independent of clock assumptions.

**Named systems.** **Chubby** (Google's lock service) is the canonical lease-based coordination primitive: clients hold session leases with the Chubby master, and Chubby-based leader election works by having candidates race to acquire a lock backed by a lease, with a sequence number attached (Chubby's analogue of a fencing token) usable by downstream services. **Spanner** uses **TrueTime**, an API exposing a bounded uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` for the current time (rather than a single timestamp), and leader leases in Spanner's Paxos groups are granted and extended such that leadership intervals of successive leaders cannot overlap even given TrueTime's epsilon uncertainty — directly using the uncertainty bound as the safety margin instead of assuming perfect clocks.

## 4. Membership Changes

Reconfiguring the member set of a replicated system without breaking safety reduces to one invariant: **any quorum of the old configuration must intersect any quorum of the new configuration** — quorum overlap across the transition — otherwise an old quorum and a new quorum could independently commit conflicting values (split-brain).

**Raft's joint consensus** satisfies this by requiring, during transition, that log entries be committed by majorities of *both* `C_old` and `C_new` simultaneously, guaranteeing overlap at every instant of the transition; the simpler **single-server-change** restriction used by most production systems achieves the same invariant implicitly because adding/removing one member from a majority-sized set cannot produce two disjoint majorities.

**Paxos-style reconfiguration** treats membership changes as just another command in the replicated log: a reconfiguration command, once chosen like any other value, takes effect some fixed number of slots later, giving a well-defined point at which the new configuration's quorums become authoritative — this delayed-activation technique avoids ambiguity about which configuration governs a given log slot.

**View-stamped replication (VR)** uses an explicit **view change** protocol: each configuration/leader epoch is a numbered **view**, and a view change (triggered by suspected leader failure) elects a new primary for a new view number, structurally similar to Raft's term-based leader election (Raft's design was in fact influenced by VR) but historically predating Raft.

**Configuration epochs/views as the general concept.** Across all these systems, the membership (and/or leadership) at any point in time is tagged with a monotonically increasing **epoch** or **view number**, and nodes always prefer the highest epoch they've observed, rejecting stale-epoch messages — this is the same mechanism as Raft's term and Zab's epoch, applied specifically to membership rather than just leadership.

**Virtually synchronous group membership** is a related but distinct model: in **virtual synchrony** (used in group communication systems like Isis), membership changes are delivered as totally-ordered events to all surviving members, and message delivery is coordinated with view changes so that all members agree on which messages were delivered in which view — a stronger, more synchronized coupling between data messages and membership events than Paxos/Raft reconfiguration typically provides.

## 5. Consistency Models

- **Linearizability**: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and response, consistent with a single global real-time total order per object; equivalent to atomic register semantics. Strongest single-object consistency model commonly implemented.
- **Sequential consistency**: there exists a total order of all operations consistent with each individual process's program order, but that order need not respect real time across processes — weaker than linearizability because it permits reordering relative to wall-clock time as long as per-process order is preserved.
- **Causal consistency**: only operations related by **happens-before** (Lamport's relation: program order plus reads-from/writes-follow dependencies, transitively closed) must be observed in the same order by everyone; concurrent (causally unrelated) operations may be observed in different orders by different replicas.
- **Eventual consistency**: guarantees only that replicas converge to the same state if updates stop arriving; makes no ordering guarantee during convergence. **CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are the named mechanism achieving **Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC)**: data types (G-Counter, OR-Set, etc.) whose merge function is proven commutative, associative, and idempotent, guaranteeing any two replicas that have seen the same set of updates converge to the identical state without coordination.
- **Session guarantees**: client-centric properties layered atop weaker base models — **read-your-writes** (a client always sees its own prior writes), **monotonic reads** (successive reads never go backward in time), **monotonic writes** (writes are serialized in the order a client issued them), **writes-follow-reads** (a write issued after a read is ordered after any writes that read observed).
- **Relation to CAP/PACELC**: linearizability is the "C" in the **CAP theorem**. **PACELC** extends CAP by noting that even absent a partition ("E", else), a system still trades latency against consistency ("LC") — e.g. synchronous quorum reads for linearizability cost latency versus serving possibly-stale local reads.

## 6. Failure Modes

A standard **failure hierarchy**, ordered from most restrictive (easiest to tolerate) to least:

- **Crash-stop (fail-stop)**: a process halts permanently and never sends further messages; other processes may or may not be able to detect this reliably.
- **Crash-recovery**: a process halts and may later restart, typically needing to recover state from persistent storage — raises the question of what survives a crash (motivating write-ahead logging/durability guarantees in Raft/Paxos before acknowledging).
- **Omission failures**: a process fails to send (**send-omission**) or fails to receive (**receive-omission**) a message it should have, while otherwise behaving correctly — weaker fault model than crash because the process keeps running.
- **Timing failures**: in a system with synchrony assumptions, a process responds correctly but outside the assumed time bound (a performance failure) — relevant because algorithms assuming synchronous bounds can violate safety, not just liveness, under timing faults.
- **Byzantine failures**: arbitrary, including malicious, behavior — a Byzantine process may send conflicting messages to different peers, lie about its state, or collude. Byzantine faults strictly subsume all the above; any protocol correct under Byzantine faults is correct under weaker fault models, but not vice versa.

**Byzantine Generals Problem and resilience bounds.** Lamport, Shostak, Pease formalized the problem of reaching agreement despite traitorous generals; the classic result is that **Byzantine agreement requires n ≥ 3f+1** total nodes to tolerate f Byzantine faults in an asynchronous or partially synchronous network (without extra cryptographic assumptions like signatures, which can relax this bound in some variants). **PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance)** is the canonical named protocol achieving this bound efficiently, using a three-phase (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) protocol per view with a primary and view-change sub-protocol analogous to VR/Raft but tolerant of Byzantine primaries.

**Partitions vs. partial/asymmetric failures.** A clean network **partition** splits nodes into disjoint groups with no cross-group communication, but connectivity within each group is normal. Real networks also exhibit **asymmetric/partial failures** — e.g. node A can send to B but not receive from B, or a link drops only some message types — which are harder to reason about because they violate the common simplifying assumption that connectivity is symmetric and binary; these are typically modeled as omission faults on individual links rather than as topology-level partitions.

## 7. Atomic Broadcast

**Definition.** **Total order broadcast** (atomic broadcast) requires: **validity** (if a correct process broadcasts a message, it eventually delivers it), **uniform agreement** (if any process, correct or not, delivers a message, all correct processes eventually deliver it), **integrity** (a message is delivered at most once, and only if actually broadcast), and **total order** (if two correct processes both deliver messages m1 and m2, they deliver them in the same relative order).

**Equivalence with consensus.** Chandra and Toueg showed atomic broadcast and consensus are **equivalent** in asynchronous systems with crash faults: atomic broadcast can be implemented by running a sequence of consensus instances (one per batch/slot of messages to be ordered), and conversely consensus can be implemented using atomic broadcast (deliver proposals in total order, decide the first delivered). This equivalence is why Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Zab — all at their core repeated-consensus engines — are naturally used to implement replicated logs/atomic broadcast primitives.

**Zab.** **Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast** implements total order broadcast with a leader-based protocol: a single leader per **epoch** proposes transactions tagged with a **zxid** (a 64-bit identifier splitting into high-order epoch number and low-order counter), followers acknowledge in a two-phase (propose, commit) exchange, and a transaction commits once acknowledged by a quorum. Epoch changes on leader failure follow a recovery phase that synchronizes the new leader's history with the highest zxid any quorum member has seen, analogous to Raft's election-restriction safety mechanism but using zxid instead of (term, index) pairs.

**Virtual synchrony.** Group communication systems built on **virtual synchrony** provide an operational relative of atomic broadcast: message delivery order is coordinated with group **view** changes such that every member that remains in a view sees the same sequence of messages and the same view transition, giving a strong agreement property similar to uniform total order broadcast but historically framed around group membership events rather than a replicated log abstraction.

## 8. Impossibility Results

**FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985).** No deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee both safety and termination in a purely **asynchronous** system (no bound on message delay or relative process speed) if even a single process can crash. The proof is an indistinguishability argument: in any run that hasn't yet decided, there's always some message delay/scheduling that keeps the system from being forced to decide, because a fully asynchronous observer can never distinguish a slow correct process from a crashed one.

**CAP theorem (Brewer's conjecture, formalized by Gilbert and Lynch).** A distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide **Consistency** (linearizability), **Availability** (every request to a non-failed node receives a response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system continues operating despite arbitrary message loss between nodes) — under an actual partition, a system must choose to sacrifice either strict consistency or availability.

**Circumventing FLP in practice.** Real systems don't defeat FLP; they sidestep the fully-asynchronous assumption or accept probabilistic/partial termination:
- **Randomization** — Ben-Or's algorithm uses randomized local coin flips so that consensus terminates with probability 1 (not deterministically), evading FLP's deterministic-algorithm precondition.
- **Unreliable failure detectors** — Chandra and Toueg define failure detector classes by accuracy/completeness properties; the weakest sufficient for consensus is **◇S** (eventually strong), and the related **Ω (Omega)** failure detector — an eventual leader-election oracle that eventually outputs the same correct process at every node — is shown to be the *weakest* failure detector for solving consensus, exactly capturing the extra power needed beyond pure asynchrony.
- **Partial synchrony** (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer model) — assumes bounds on message delay and clock drift that hold eventually or after some unknown point, rather than always; this is the formal model underlying the practical liveness arguments of Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Zab, all of which guarantee safety always but liveness only under partial synchrony (hence randomized election timeouts in Raft as an engineering proxy for eventual synchrony).

# 1. Raft

Raft decomposes replicated state machine consensus into three largely independent subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety. It is designed for understandability, replacing Paxos's single-decree consensus abstraction with a strong-leader, log-centric model in which all client commands flow through one leader at a time.

## 1.1 Server states and terms

Every server is in one of three states: **leader**, **follower**, or **candidate**. Time is divided into **terms**, monotonically increasing integers that act as a logical clock. Each term begins with an election; it has at most one leader (possibly none, if an election fails to produce a majority winner, i.e. a "split vote"). Each server persists `currentTerm` and advances it whenever it observes a higher term in an RPC. A server that sees a higher term in any message immediately reverts to follower state — this is the mechanism by which **stale leaders are detected and demoted**: an old leader partitioned from the majority will, upon healing, receive an AppendEntries or RequestVote carrying a newer term and step down. Terms are included in every RPC and every reply; a server rejects any RPC bearing a stale term.

## 1.2 Leader election

Followers expect periodic **AppendEntries** heartbeats from the leader. Each follower maintains an **election timeout** (typically 150–300 ms) chosen **randomly** on each reset. If no heartbeat arrives before the timeout expires, the follower increments `currentTerm`, transitions to candidate, votes for itself, and issues parallel **RequestVote RPCs** to all other servers, carrying `(term, candidateId, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm)`.

A server grants its vote (returns `voteGranted=true`) only if:
1. The candidate's term is ≥ its own `currentTerm` (and it updates `currentTerm` accordingly),
2. It has not already voted for a different candidate in that term (`votedFor` persisted to stable storage, reset each new term), and
3. The candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own, per the **election restriction** below.

A candidate becomes leader upon receiving votes from a **majority (quorum)** of the cluster (`⌈(n+1)/2⌉` of `n` servers). Randomized timeouts make split votes unlikely to recur: with high probability one server times out meaningfully before others, wins the term outright, and sends heartbeats before others' timers expire, suppressing further elections. Raft requires a majority quorum for both election and commitment, guaranteeing any two quorums intersect in at least one server — the basis for all of Raft's safety arguments.

## 1.3 Log replication

Client commands are appended as **log entries** `(term, index, command)` to the leader's log, then replicated via **AppendEntries RPCs**, parameterized by `(term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit)`.

**Log Matching Property**: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then (a) they store the same command, and (b) the logs are identical in all preceding entries. This is enforced constructively: a leader never overwrites or reorders its own log, only appends; and AppendEntries includes a consistency check — the follower rejects the RPC unless its log already contains an entry at `prevLogIndex` with term `prevLogTerm`. On rejection, the leader decrements `nextIndex` for that follower and retries (implementations commonly batch-skip using the conflicting term/index returned by the follower rather than one entry at a time). When a follower does accept new entries, it deletes any conflicting entries already present at those indices before appending the leader's entries — overwriting divergent follower logs rather than leader logs.

The leader tracks, for each follower, `matchIndex` (highest index known replicated) and `nextIndex` (next entry to send). An entry is considered **committed** once it is stored on a **majority** of servers' logs; the leader advances its `commitIndex` to the highest index for which this majority-match condition holds, **and which was replicated during the leader's own current term** (see §1.4). The leader then applies the entry to its state machine and informs followers of the new `commitIndex` via subsequent AppendEntries (`leaderCommit` field), driving their own application of committed entries in log order. Committed entries are durable: they survive leader crashes and will appear in the log of every future leader.

## 1.4 Safety: election restriction and Leader Completeness

Raft's central safety invariant is the **Leader Completeness Property**: if a log entry is committed in a given term, it will be present in the logs of all leaders of all subsequent terms.

This is guaranteed by the **election restriction** embedded in RequestVote: a voter denies its vote unless the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own, where "up-to-date" is determined by comparing `(lastLogTerm, lastLogIndex)` lexicographically — higher last term wins; if tied, longer log wins. Because any committed entry must have been acknowledged by a majority, and any candidate must win votes from a majority, every successful candidate's voter-quorum intersects the quorum that committed the entry in at least one server. That server, having the committed entry, will refuse to vote for a candidate whose log doesn't already contain it (since the entry's term is ≤ the server's own `lastLogTerm` region and index comparison fails for any candidate missing it). Hence every elected leader already holds all previously committed entries — no committed entry is ever lost or rolled back.

A subtlety: a leader cannot conclude an entry is committed merely because it's replicated on a majority **if that entry was from a previous term**. Raft never commits entries from older terms by counting replicas directly; instead, a new leader's first act is implicitly to let a new entry from its *own* term reach a majority, which indirectly commits all preceding entries via the Log Matching Property (prefix consistency). This avoids the figure-8 scenario in the Raft paper where an entry replicated on a majority in a prior term could, under naive counting, later be overwritten by a different leader.

## 1.5 Membership changes

**Joint consensus**: the original Raft paper's approach for arbitrary configuration changes. The cluster transitions through a special log entry `C_old,new` combining old and new configurations; during this joint phase, both the old and new configurations' majorities are independently required for election and commitment (quorums are intersected across *both* configurations), preventing two disjoint majorities (one under `C_old`, one under `C_new`) from each electing a leader independently. Only after `C_old,new` is committed does the leader append and commit a final `C_new` entry, after which the old-configuration requirement is dropped. No window exists where two leaders can be elected under fully disjoint configurations.

**Single-server changes**: the practically favored simplification (used in the Raft dissertation and most production implementations, e.g. etcd). Because any single addition or removal of one server cannot produce two disjoint majorities when old and new configurations overlap by at least one server, changes are restricted to adding/removing one server at a time, applied as a normal committed log entry — eliminating the need for the two-phase joint configuration entirely. Arbitrary configuration changes are achieved by composing a sequence of single-server changes.

New servers joining with empty logs are typically brought in as **non-voting learners** first, catching up via normal log replication before being promoted to voting members, to avoid availability gaps caused by slow catch-up during the quorum-sensitive window.

## 1.6 Log compaction via snapshotting

Since the log grows unboundedly, each server independently takes **snapshots**: a complete copy of current state machine state together with `lastIncludedIndex` and `lastIncludedTerm`, after which the log prefix up to that index can be discarded. A leader may send an `InstallSnapshot RPC` to a slow or newly added follower that has fallen far behind (i.e. the leader has already compacted away entries the follower needs), transferring the snapshot in chunks and resetting the follower's log to begin at `lastIncludedIndex`. Snapshotting is an implementation/performance mechanism, orthogonal to the core safety protocol — it does not alter commit or election semantics, only truncates which prefix of history must be retained and transferred.

---

# 2. Paxos and Variants

## 2.1 Basic Paxos

Basic Paxos solves **single-decree** consensus: a set of processes agree on exactly one value, tolerating crash failures (and message loss, with asynchronous timing — no clock synchrony assumed), provided a majority of participants remain reachable.

Roles: **Proposer**, **Acceptor**, **Learner** (a single physical process can play multiple roles). Each proposal is tagged with a **proposal number** (also called a **ballot number**), drawn from a totally ordered, proposer-unique domain (commonly `(round, proposerId)` pairs to guarantee global uniqueness without coordination).

**Phase 1 (Prepare/Promise)**:
- Proposer selects a proposal number `n` higher than any it has used before, sends `Prepare(n)` to a majority (quorum) of acceptors.
- An acceptor receiving `Prepare(n)`, if `n` is greater than any proposal number it has already responded to, replies with `Promise(n, acceptedProposal)` — where `acceptedProposal` is the highest-numbered proposal (if any) it has already *accepted* (i.e. `(n', v')`) — and promises never again to accept any proposal numbered less than `n`. If `n` is not greater than one already promised, it ignores or NACKs the request.

**Phase 2 (Accept/Accepted)**:
- If the proposer receives Promise responses from a majority, it must choose a value `v`: if any acceptor in its responses reported a previously accepted value, the proposer must adopt the value associated with the **highest-numbered** such accepted proposal (safety-critical — it cannot pick an arbitrary new value once any acceptor has already accepted something under a lower, promised-over proposal number). Otherwise, it may propose a value of its own choosing.
- The proposer sends `Accept(n, v)` to a quorum of acceptors.
- An acceptor accepts (and records) `(n, v)` unless it has already promised a higher-numbered proposal in the meantime; it replies `Accepted(n, v)`.
- Once a majority of acceptors accept the same `(n, v)`, `v` is **chosen**; learners discover this by querying acceptors or being notified directly.

**Safety via quorum intersection**: any two majority quorums of acceptors intersect in at least one acceptor. This is the mechanism that prevents two different values from being chosen under different proposal numbers: if `v` is chosen at proposal `n`, any later proposal `n' > n` must obtain promises from a quorum that intersects the accepting quorum of `n`; that intersecting acceptor will report its previously accepted `(n, v)` in its Promise reply, forcing any subsequent higher-numbered proposal to also carry `v` forward. This inductive argument is Paxos's P2c invariant and is the core safety proof technique shared conceptually with Raft's election restriction (both are quorum-intersection arguments, differing in mechanism: log comparison in Raft vs. "adopt highest accepted value" in Paxos).

Paxos tolerates up to `f` acceptor failures with `2f+1` acceptors, needing a quorum of `f+1`.

## 2.2 Why Basic Paxos alone doesn't give state machine replication

Basic Paxos as specified decides a *single* value once. To replicate a log (state machine replication, SMR), one logically needs an independent instance of Paxos per log slot/index. Running fully independent Basic Paxos instances per slot has severe costs:

- Every instance requires its own Phase 1 (Prepare/Promise) round-trip before any value can even be proposed, doubling latency (two round trips instead of one) for every single command.
- Multiple proposers can collide, triggering repeated **dueling proposers** — if two proposers interleave Prepare requests with ever-higher proposal numbers, neither value may ever be chosen (liveness failure, consistent with Paxos not solving consensus in a model subject to the FLP impossibility result without resorting to randomization, leader election, or other external liveness assumptions, since pure asynchronous consensus has no deterministic always-live solution).
- There is no inherent mechanism in Basic Paxos tying separate single-decree instances together into an ordered, gap-free, replicated log; it only answers "what single value was chosen," not "how do we efficiently and continuously agree on a stream of values in order with liveness under a stable but unidentified leader."

**Multi-Paxos** is the (informally specified, implementation-defined) extension that actually yields practical SMR.

## 2.3 Multi-Paxos

Key optimization: elect (or allow to emerge) a **distinguished proposer** (a stable leader) that persists across many log slots. Once a proposer's Phase 1 Prepare has been accepted by a quorum for proposal number `n` *and no competing higher-numbered proposal appears*, that same proposer can **skip Phase 1 for all future slots**, issuing only Phase 2 Accept messages directly — because the Promise from Phase 1 already covers "no acceptor will accept anything lower-numbered than `n`," which can be interpreted (with suitable bookkeeping, e.g. a single Prepare covering an open-ended range of future instances, as in the original Lamport "Part-time Parliament" treatment, or re-running Prepare only after leader change) as blanket permission to propose values at that ballot number for subsequent slots without renegotiating Phase 1 per slot.

This collapses steady-state replication to a **single round trip** (just Accept/Accepted) per committed entry — structurally identical in message-complexity to Raft's steady-state AppendEntries. The distinguished proposer role is exactly analogous to Raft's leader; the proposal/ballot number is exactly analogous to Raft's term; the quorum-based promise mechanism is analogous to the election restriction, though expressed via "highest accepted value adoption" rather than "longest/most up-to-date log."

Leader election/leader lease mechanisms (how a proposer becomes "distinguished" and how competing proposers back off) are left outside strict Paxos specification; practical systems (e.g. Google's Chubby, Spanner's use of Paxos groups) layer leader leases, timeouts and randomized backoff atop Multi-Paxos much as Raft specifies natively.

## 2.4 Fast Paxos

**Fast Paxos** (Lamport) reduces end-to-end latency by allowing certain rounds to skip the leader-mediated path entirely. In a **fast round**, any proposer (actually, effectively any client) can send its value directly to a quorum of acceptors — a **fast quorum**, which must be sized larger than a simple majority (specifically, with `N` acceptors, classic quorum size `⌊N/2⌋+1`, but fast quorums require a size such that any two fast quorums intersect sufficiently to guarantee at most one value could "win" without leader arbitration; commonly `⌈2N/3⌉`-style sizing or more precisely the quorum sizing must satisfy `Q_f ≥ ⌈(N+Q_c+1)/2⌉`-style intersection constraints relative to the classic quorum `Q_c`). This collapses the normal 3-message-delay Paxos path to 2 message delays in the common case (client → acceptors → learners) by eliding the leader's mediation of Phase 2.

The cost is **collisions**: if multiple clients submit different values concurrently in the same fast round, no single value may achieve the required fast-quorum majority, and the round fails to choose a value. Fast Paxos requires a **collision recovery** phase, essentially falling back to classic Paxos mediation (a coordinator collects the conflicting accepted values and resolves via a subsequent classic round, using an appropriate recovery rule to pick among colliding values) — trading a lower-latency common case for an extra round-trip penalty on contention. Fast Paxos illustrates a fundamental latency/contention-tolerance trade-off absent from leader-funneled Multi-Paxos or Raft, where all proposals are serialized through one leader and therefore never collide at the ordering layer (though they still compete for the leader's attention, a scheduling rather than consensus-safety issue).

## 2.5 Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos) — brief contrast

EPaxos removes the distinguished-leader bottleneck entirely: it is **leaderless**, allowing *any* replica to opportunistically propose and commit a command in as few as one round trip to a **fast quorum**, in the common case. Instead of enforcing a single global total order via a sequencer/leader, EPaxos tracks **interference/dependencies** among commands: each command, upon being proposed, is attached with the set of commands it depends on (commands it does not commute with, learned from the replicas' recent history), and replicas execute a dependency graph respecting these pairwise orderings via a form of topological ordering (e.g. a Tarjan-style SCC-ordering execution) rather than requiring one global sequence number. This trades leader bottleneck/single point of serialization for more complex conflict and dependency bookkeeping (and more costly recovery when dependency sets must be reconciled under failures), and it only requires reordering/serializing commands that actually conflict — commutative or disjoint commands can be applied in different orders on different replicas with the same final state, improving throughput and avoiding leader hot-spotting and wide-area latency penalties tied to a fixed leader location.

## 2.6 Cheap Paxos — brief note

Cheap Paxos reduces steady-state hardware cost: with `2F+1` acceptors normally needed to tolerate `F` failures, Cheap Paxos uses only `F+1` "main" acceptors actively participating in steady state, with `F` additional low-cost standby "auxiliary" acceptors that are only activated (brought online, at the cost of an extra reconfiguration round) when a main acceptor actually fails — paying the full `2F+1` participation cost only during failure recovery rather than continuously, at the expense of a brief extra latency/availability hit during reconfiguration after a failure.

---

# 3. Atomic Broadcast

## 3.1 Definition (Total Order Broadcast)

**Atomic broadcast** (equivalently **total order broadcast**, TOB) is a group communication primitive providing two operations, `broadcast(m)` and `deliver(m)`, satisfying:

- **Validity**: if a correct process broadcasts a message `m`, then it eventually delivers `m` (liveness, assuming the broadcaster doesn't crash).
- **Uniform Agreement**: if any process (correct or not, "uniform" strengthening) delivers `m`, then all correct processes eventually deliver `m`.
- **Integrity**: every message is delivered by any given process at most once, and only if it was previously broadcast (no spurious or duplicate delivery).
- **Total Order** (often stated as uniform total order): if two correct processes both deliver messages `m` and `m'`, they deliver them in the **same relative order**.

Atomic broadcast is strictly stronger than reliable broadcast (which provides agreement/validity/integrity but no ordering guarantee) and is the communication-layer analogue of achieving a single, globally agreed, append-only sequence of operations — precisely what a replicated log needs for **linearizability** of the replicated state machine, provided clients wait for delivery confirmation before treating operations as complete.

## 3.2 Equivalence with Consensus (Chandra–Toueg direction)

Chandra and Toueg (building on prior folklore results) established that **atomic broadcast and consensus are equivalent** in asynchronous systems augmented with failure detectors: each can be implemented given the other, and conversely each inherits the other's impossibility/necessary-condition structure.

- **Consensus ⇒ Atomic Broadcast**: given a consensus primitive, atomic broadcast can be built by having processes repeatedly batch pending broadcast messages into rounds, running one consensus instance per round to agree on the *set* (or sequence) of messages to deliver next, then delivering them in a deterministic order (e.g. sorted by message ID) agreed by that consensus instance. This is essentially what Multi-Paxos / Raft do: successive consensus decisions on log slots directly yield a totally ordered delivery sequence.
- **Atomic Broadcast ⇒ Consensus**: given atomic broadcast, consensus can be built trivially — each process broadcasts its proposed value, and all processes decide on the **first value** they atomically deliver. Agreement and total order of the broadcast primitive directly imply that all correct processes agree on the same first-delivered value, i.e. consensus.

This bidirectional reducibility is the **Chandra–Toueg equivalence**: the two problems are computationally equivalent in asynchronous systems with crash failures, and both are subject to the same **FLP impossibility** result in purely asynchronous systems without failure detectors — neither is solvable deterministically with guaranteed termination without some additional timing/failure-detector assumption (e.g. a ◇S or ◇W failure detector, partial synchrony, randomization, or a leader-election oracle).

## 3.3 Zab (Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast)

**Zab** is the atomic broadcast protocol underlying Apache ZooKeeper, purpose-built (unlike generic Paxos) to support the exact primary-backup state machine replication pattern ZooKeeper needs, including recovery of in-flight proposals after a leader (primary) crash.

Core mechanisms:

- **Leader-based**: Zab designates a single **leader** (chosen by a separate, Zab-internal **fast leader election** sub-protocol) through which all state-changing operations are funneled, analogous to Raft's leader and Multi-Paxos's distinguished proposer.
- **Epoch**: each leader generation is tagged with a monotonically increasing **epoch number**, directly analogous to a Raft **term** or Paxos **ballot number**. A new leader, upon election, establishes a new epoch strictly greater than any epoch seen by a quorum of followers.
- **zxid**: every transaction (state-changing proposal) is assigned a globally unique, monotonically increasing 64-bit **zxid** (ZooKeeper transaction ID), structurally composed of `(epoch, counter)` — the high-order bits encode the epoch, the low-order bits a counter reset to zero at the start of each epoch. zxids thus provide a total order consistent with epochs: any zxid from a later epoch is ordered after all zxids from earlier epochs, and within an epoch the counter gives a strict sequence.
- **Protocol phases**: Zab proceeds through (1) **leader election**, (2) **discovery** (the prospective leader learns the highest zxid/epoch known by a quorum of followers, to ensure it doesn't lose previously-delivered transactions — analogous to Raft's election restriction / Paxos's "adopt highest accepted value"), (3) **synchronization** (the leader brings followers up to date with any transactions they're missing before normal operation begins, analogous to Raft's log catch-up via AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot), and (4) **broadcast** (the steady-state phase: the leader proposes transactions with sequential zxids, followers ack, and once a quorum acks, the leader commits and notifies followers to deliver/apply the transaction in zxid order).
- Zab guarantees a stronger **primary order** property beyond generic atomic broadcast: if a leader broadcasts transaction `T` before `T'` (as the active primary), every server delivers `T` before `T'`; and it specifically guarantees that any transaction delivered by any server was created by the most recent leader that generated it, with correct causal/epoch recovery semantics to handle leader failures mid-broadcast cleanly.

Zab and Multi-Paxos/Raft solve essentially the same ordering problem; Zab's distinguishing design choice is its explicit `(epoch, counter)`-structured zxid replacing a generic integer term/ballot plus a separate log index, and its specialized recovery (discovery/synchronization) phases tailored to ZooKeeper's primary-backup implementation rather than being derived generically from a Paxos specification.

## 3.4 Virtual Synchrony and Group Communication Systems

**Virtual synchrony**, originating from the Isis system (Birman et al.), is a broader group communication model historically predating and partially overlapping atomic broadcast. Its central guarantee ties message delivery to **group membership views**: all members that remain in the same **view** (an agreed, totally ordered sequence of membership-change events — joins, leaves, failures) observe the same set of messages delivered within that view, and view changes themselves are delivered consistently to all surviving members "as if" simultaneously (hence "virtual synchrony" — the system behaves as though message delivery and view changes were instantaneous and globally agreed, even though physically they're asynchronous).

Virtual synchrony typically bundles several ordering properties of differing strength: **FIFO order**, **causal order**, and optionally **total order** (the latter being exactly atomic broadcast layered within a given view). The relationship: atomic broadcast as defined in §3.1 is essentially the **totally-ordered delivery guarantee restricted to a single, static membership**; virtual synchrony generalizes this by additionally specifying how delivery guarantees compose across dynamic **view changes** — e.g., guaranteeing that a message is either delivered to all members of a view before the view changes, or to none of the surviving members (a safety property sometimes called **view synchrony** or **virtually synchronous delivery**).

In practice, systems providing virtual synchrony (Isis, Horus, Ensemble, Spread) implement atomic/total-order broadcast as one of several selectable delivery qualities-of-service within the membership-view framework, whereas Zab/Multi-Paxos/Raft achieve an equivalent effect by folding membership changes directly into the replicated log/epoch mechanism itself (configuration-change entries in Raft; epoch changes plus discovery/synchronization in Zab) rather than treating group membership as a logically separate layer beneath ordered message delivery. The two traditions converge on the same underlying requirement — consistent total order coupled with consistent handling of membership/leadership changes — but structure the abstraction boundary differently: virtual synchrony factors out "views" as a first-class, general-purpose membership abstraction usable by multiple communication qualities of service (including weaker-than-total orders), while the consensus-replication tradition (Raft/Paxos/Zab) treats membership change as just another entry in the same totally-ordered log that carries application commands.

# Lease-Based Coordination

## The Lease Abstraction

A lease is a time-bounded grant of an exclusive right, issued by a granter (typically a coordination service or consensus-backed authority) to a holder. Unlike a plain distributed lock, which is held until explicitly released, a lease carries an expiration time negotiated in advance. This bounds the duration of any safety violation caused by a holder that fails, hangs, or becomes partitioned: once the lease's term elapses, the granter is free to issue the right to someone else, and correctness protocols can assume the old holder is no longer authorized without requiring it to acknowledge revocation.

Leases are used for several related purposes:

- **Leadership / mastership**: only the lease holder may act as leader, primary, or master for a given epoch.
- **Cache ownership / client caching**: a server grants a client a lease on cached data, promising to notify the client of invalidations for the lease term, or to block conflicting writes until the lease expires (Chubby's "cache lease" use case for client-side caching of file/lock metadata).
- **Exclusive write access to a resource/shard**, common in sharded storage systems where a single owner per shard avoids coordination overhead on every write.

The key property distinguishing a lease from a lock is **time-bounding under a shared notion of time**, which is exactly what introduces the clock-synchronization concerns below.

## Clock Synchronization Assumptions

A lease's safety property — "at most one holder considers the lease valid at any instant" — depends on the granter's and holder's clocks agreeing closely enough that their respective notions of "lease has expired" don't diverge pathologically.

Concretely:

- The granter stamps the lease with an expiration time `T_expire = T_grant + duration`, measured on its own clock.
- The holder must stop relying on the lease by some local deadline it computes, typically earlier than `T_expire` by a safety margin, to account for request latency, clock drift, and scheduling delay between when it last confirmed validity and when it acts.
- **Safety depends on bounded clock drift**: if the holder's clock runs slow relative to the granter's, the holder may believe the lease is still valid after the granter has already expired it and granted it to someone else — producing two simultaneous holders. If clocks are only loosely synchronized (bounded skew ε, not perfectly synchronized), the holder's effective "safe to act until" time must be `T_grant_local + duration - 2ε` (or some such margin derived from the maximum possible skew and message delay), not the raw expiration time.
- This is why lease-based protocols require an explicit, quantified bound on clock drift/skew between participants (even if that bound is generous, e.g. milliseconds to seconds). Unbounded or unknown clock drift makes the lease abstraction unsafe regardless of lease duration, because no fixed safety margin can be proven sufficient.
- Practical systems manage this via: NTP-synchronized clocks with conservative assumed-maximum-skew constants (Chubby's original design), or hardware/infrastructure-level engineering to bound skew tightly and expose the uncertainty explicitly (Spanner's TrueTime).

**Spanner's TrueTime** is the most rigorous named mechanism here: instead of returning a single timestamp, the TrueTime API returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain the true time, with a bounded uncertainty `ε` (typically single-digit milliseconds, kept small via GPS and atomic clock references in each datacenter plus a time-master hierarchy). Spanner's leader leases are granted and extended based on TrueTime intervals: a leader proves it holds a lease until some absolute time by ensuring its lease interval's lower bound exceeds the current TrueTime upper bound by the required margin, and a new leader cannot be elected until the old leader's lease is guaranteed (via TrueTime's uncertainty bound) to have expired. This lets Spanner reason about lease disjointness as a provable interval-overlap property rather than an empirical assumption about clock skew.

## Lease Renewal and Expiration

- **Renewal**: before expiration, the holder proactively requests an extension. The granter, if it still considers the holder valid (no competing claim, no failure detected), issues a new lease with a later expiration, usually without any gap in coverage as long as the renewal round-trip completes before the old lease's safety margin is exhausted.
- **Expiration without renewal**: if the holder fails to renew in time, the granter may unilaterally consider the lease void, select a new holder, and no longer honor operations attributed to the old lease — even if the old holder is still alive and unaware that it lost the lease.
- **Grace periods**: some systems (Chubby) add a grace period during which a client that misses a keep-alive can attempt to reclaim its session before it's torn down, to tolerate transient network issues without triggering unnecessary mastership churn.
- **Session-based leases**: in Chubby and ZooKeeper, the lease is not attached to a single lock but to a **session**, which aggregates all locks/ephemeral state held by a client. The session has a single lease duration; a missed heartbeat (KeepAlive in Chubby, ping in ZooKeeper) within the session timeout causes the session — and everything it holds — to expire atomically.

## Leases for Leader Election / Mastership

**Chubby** (Google's lock service, Paxos-replicated internally) provides advisory locks plus a session mechanism. A common pattern: candidates race to acquire a lock file (e.g. `/ls/cell/service/master`); the winner holds the lock as long as its session lease is renewed, and writes its identity into the file content for others to discover. Losing the lock (session expiry, explicit release, or Chubby master failover exceeding the session timeout) means the client must assume it is no longer master. Chubby deliberately keeps the coordination primitive (locks + small reliable storage) general rather than baking in leader election directly, but leader election is its most common application.

**ZooKeeper** provides a similar model via ephemeral znodes tied to a client session. A typical leader election recipe: all candidates attempt to create an ephemeral (and often sequential) znode under an election path; the session lease is maintained by periodic heartbeats to the ZooKeeper ensemble; if the session times out (missed heartbeats beyond `sessionTimeout`), the ephemeral znode is deleted, signaling to watchers that the leader slot is vacant. Leadership is thus derived from "my ephemeral znode still exists," which is a session-lease-backed, not independently-timed, lease.

In both systems, the crucial availability/safety tradeoff is the **session timeout duration**: too short causes spurious mastership changes under transient slowness (GC pauses, network blips); too long delays failover after a genuine failure.

## Zombie Leaders and Fencing Tokens

**The zombie/fenced-out leader problem**: a leader's lease can expire from the granter's point of view while the leader itself is still alive and still believes it holds the lease. Common causes:

- A long stop-the-world (STW) garbage collection pause during which the process cannot renew its lease in time, but resumes execution afterward unaware that time has passed.
- A network partition that prevents renewal messages from reaching the granter, while the leader's own clock/process continues running normally.
- OS-level scheduling delays, swapping, or hypervisor preemption in virtualized/cloud environments.

When this happens, the granter has already handed the lease to a new leader, but the old leader — a "zombie" — may still issue writes to downstream resources (storage, a database, other services) believing it is authoritative. If the zombie's writes are not blocked, you get **split-brain**: two leaders concurrently mutating shared state, violating single-writer safety invariants.

**Fencing tokens** solve this independently of the lease timing itself, by having downstream resources — not just the leader — enforce recency. The mechanism:

- Each time a lease is granted (or renewed to a new holder, i.e., on leadership change), the granter issues a monotonically increasing **fencing token** (a sequence number, often called an **epoch number** or **generation number**) along with the lease.
- The leader must present this token with every write/operation to downstream resources (storage systems, other services the leader mutates).
- The downstream resource remembers the highest token number it has seen and **rejects any operation carrying a token lower than the maximum it has already observed**.
- A zombie leader, even if it is unaware its lease expired, will present a stale (lower) token than the token the new leader is using, and its writes will be rejected by any resource that enforces the monotonic-token invariant.

This converts an availability/liveness problem (detecting a zombie leader promptly) into a strict safety invariant enforced at the point of effect (the shared resource), which is much more robust than trying to make failure detection itself instantaneous. It is the standard mitigation discussed in the context of distributed locks (e.g. Martin Kleppmann's critique of naive Redis-based locking without fencing) and is used in practice in systems like GFS/Colossus chunk lease renewal, HDFS NameNode failover (generation stamps), and Spanner (which uses TrueTime-derived epoch/lease intervals rather than relying solely on tokens, since the interval-based proof of disjointness serves an analogous role).

## Named Concrete Mechanisms Recap

- **Chubby**: Paxos-replicated lock service; advisory locks + sessions with lease-based keep-alives; grace period on missed keep-alives; used pervasively at Google for leader election and small-scale coordinated metadata (e.g. GFS master election).
- **ZooKeeper**: session-based ephemeral znodes; session timeout acts as the lease; sequential znodes commonly combined with watches to implement leader election and barriers.
- **Spanner / TrueTime**: `Tinterval = [earliest, latest]` with bounded uncertainty ε; leader leases proven disjoint across epochs by waiting out the uncertainty interval before allowing a new leader's lease to begin, giving provable (not just empirically assumed) mutual exclusion across clock skew.

# Membership Changes

## The General Problem

A replicated system's safety (no two conflicting values committed for the same slot/key, no lost acknowledged writes) rests on **quorum**-based agreement: a write or decision is considered durable once acknowledged by a quorum (commonly a majority) of the current configuration's members. Reconfiguration — changing which servers constitute the replica set, adding/removing/replacing members — is dangerous because it changes what counts as a quorum. If done naively, it's possible for a decision to be considered committed under one quorum definition while a conflicting decision is considered committed under another, because the two quorums never overlapped and so never had to agree with each other.

The invariant that must hold throughout any reconfiguration:

### Quorum Overlap / Quorum Intersection Requirement

**Any quorum of the old configuration (Cold) and any quorum of the new configuration (Cnew) must intersect in at least one member.** This guarantees that any decision committed under Cold is visible to (and cannot be silently overridden by) any quorum operating under Cnew, because at least one member present in both quorums carries forward knowledge of the committed decision. Violating this invariant is precisely what causes **split-brain**: two disjoint groups, each believing it holds a legitimate quorum, making independent and possibly conflicting decisions.

For simple majority quorums over a fixed-size cluster, intersection is automatic (any two majorities of the same set overlap). The problem arises specifically when the *set itself* changes between the two quorums being compared.

## Raft's Approach

**Joint consensus**: Raft's general reconfiguration mechanism transitions through an intermediate configuration `Cold,new` that is the union of the old and new member sets, during which:
- A quorum must be a majority of **both** Cold and Cnew independently (not just a majority of the union) for any decision — log entries, elections — to be considered committed.
- Because any majority-of-Cold-and-Cnew quorum necessarily contains a majority of Cold, and separately a majority of Cnew, any two such "joint" quorums intersect in Cold and intersect in Cnew, preserving quorum intersection with respect to both configurations simultaneously.
- Once `Cold,new` is itself committed (replicated to a joint-quorum), the leader can transition to `Cnew` directly, since from that point only `Cnew`'s quorums matter and the joint stage already guaranteed no decision made under `Cold,new` conflicts with what `Cnew` will see.

**Single-server membership change restriction**: in practice, the Raft paper and most production Raft implementations (etcd, Consul's underlying Raft library) use a simpler restricted protocol: **only one server may be added or removed at a time**, and only after the previous change has fully committed. The key property exploited is that any majority of a configuration of size N and any majority of a configuration differing by exactly one member (size N or N±1) always overlap, so pairwise single-server changes preserve quorum intersection without needing the explicit joint-consensus machinery. Arbitrary multi-member reconfigurations are achieved by decomposing them into a sequence of single-server changes. This is simpler to implement correctly (avoiding the dual-quorum bookkeeping of joint consensus) at the cost of requiring multiple sequential steps and committing an intermediate configuration between each.

## Paxos-Style Reconfiguration

Classic (multi-)Paxos-based systems achieve reconfiguration by treating the configuration itself as **state replicated through the log**: a special reconfiguration command is proposed and committed like any other log entry, specifying the new member set. The key design decision is **when the new configuration takes effect relative to the log position of the reconfiguration command itself** — commonly, the new configuration becomes effective some fixed number of log slots after the reconfiguration command's own slot (rather than immediately), so that the window during which members might disagree about which configuration governs a given slot is bounded and well-defined, and leaders mid-flight don't have ambiguity about which quorum rule applies to in-progress proposals. This is the approach taken in Lamport's "Paxos Made Simple"-era writings on reconfiguration and systems derived from it (e.g. the approach used in some Chubby/Paxos-replicated log implementations), and is analogous conceptually to Raft's joint-consensus staging but implemented as log-embedded configuration-change commands rather than a distinct two-phase protocol.

## Configuration Epochs / Views

Across these approaches, it's standard to tag each configuration with a monotonically increasing **epoch number** or **view number** (also called generation number or configuration version). This serves multiple purposes:
- Disambiguating which configuration a given quorum vote or log entry was made under, which is essential for implementing the staged transitions above correctly.
- Acting as a fencing mechanism analogous to lease fencing tokens: a message or vote carrying a stale epoch number can be rejected by recipients who have already moved to a higher epoch, preventing a partitioned-off minority still running the old configuration from making progress that conflicts with the majority that has since reconfigured.
- Providing a total order over configuration changes even when the underlying consensus log entries that caused them might be processed with some latency by different members.

## View-Stamped Replication (VSR)

View-Stamped Replication, one of the earliest primary-backup consensus protocols (predating and conceptually overlapping with Paxos), structures time into **views**, each with a designated primary. A **view change** occurs when the current primary is suspected failed (via timeout) or when the group needs to reconfigure; a view change protocol elects a new primary for the next view number and ensures the new primary has the longest/most up-to-date log among a quorum of participants before resuming normal operation. View numbers serve the same epoch-like fencing role: operations and view-change messages are tagged with the view number, and a replica rejects messages tagged with a view number lower than the highest it has seen (analogous to Raft's term numbers). Classic VSR handles reconfiguration of the group membership itself as a special case layered on top of the view-change mechanism; later revisions of VSR (as presented in Liskov and Cowling's updated treatment) address repeated/overlapping failures and explicitly discuss membership reconfiguration as logically distinct from ordinary view changes (which only change the primary within a fixed membership), since changing the membership set requires the same quorum-overlap reasoning applied above rather than just a leader hand-off within a static set of replicas.

## Vertical vs. Horizontal Scaling Considerations

- **Vertical scaling** (replacing a member with a more capable machine, same role, same count) is reconfiguration-light from the quorum-intersection standpoint: it's a single-server replace, handled by the standard add-one/remove-one sequence (add the new, wait for it to catch up and commit, then remove the old), and does not change quorum size or fault-tolerance characteristics.
- **Horizontal scaling** (changing the number of replicas, e.g. 3→5 for increased fault tolerance, or sharding/resharding a dataset across more participants) has more significant implications:
  - Changing replica count changes the **quorum size** and therefore the fault-tolerance threshold (a 5-node majority quorum tolerates 2 failures vs. 1 for a 3-node cluster); the reconfiguration protocol must ensure this transition doesn't create a window where an old quorum size's decision can be overridden by a differently-sized new quorum that doesn't overlap it, which is exactly why joint consensus / sequential single-node changes exist.
  - Resharding (horizontal partitioning across more shards, each potentially independently replicated) is a related but distinct problem from single-group membership change: it involves splitting or merging the keyspace/ownership in addition to changing replica sets, often requiring its own epoch/generation mechanism per shard (as in Google's Megastore, Bigtable tablet reassignment, or MongoDB's chunk migration), with ownership epochs used to fence stale replicas or stale shard-owners from acting on data they no longer own after a shard boundary move.

## Virtually Synchronous Group Membership (Related but Distinct)

**Virtual synchrony**, as introduced in the Isis Toolkit and related group communication systems, provides a different flavor of membership coordination: it guarantees that all members agree on an ordered sequence of **views** (membership lists) and that multicast messages are delivered consistently with respect to view boundaries — specifically, that all surviving members deliver the same set of messages before a given view change, i.e., messages are not delivered "across" a view boundary inconsistently among members. This is a weaker/different guarantee than quorum-based consensus reconfiguration: virtual synchrony is primarily about **consistent ordering and agreement on membership views for multicast delivery semantics** (useful for replicated group communication, publish-subscribe-style systems), not necessarily about maintaining a single global total order of all operations with quorum-intersection-guaranteed safety across arbitrary network partitions the way Paxos/Raft/VSR reconfiguration does. Virtually synchronous systems can tolerate a view change admitting a new membership agreed upon by the current view's members without the same quorum-overlap proof obligations as Raft/Paxos because they generally assume a primary-partition model (progress only in the partition that can form a sufficient view) rather than Paxos/Raft's purely quorum-counted membership overlap reasoning — the two models solve related but non-identical problems and should not be conflated.
